findings.issue_text: Missing test changes or validation evidence for changed source files: `lib/post_creator.rb`, `lib/post_revisor.rb`, `lib/tasks/disqus.thor`, and `lib/topic_retriever.rb`.
app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 — `import_remote` uses `open(url)` without requiring `open-uri` on the normal retrieval path, so HTTP URLs may be treated as local filenames.

[lens/completeness] spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:43 — The test expects synchronous `TopicRetriever.new(...).retrieve`, while the controller now enqueues `:retrieve_topic`; the test fails and does not validate the asynchronous handoff.
app/models/topic_embed.rb:11 — URL validation checks only an `http(s)://` prefix, so malformed values such as `http://[` pass and later raise instead of being rejected cleanly.

app/models/topic_embed.rb:64 — URL absolutization handles only root-relative paths; document-relative references such as `article/2`, `../images/x.png`, and `?page=2` resolve against Discourse instead of the source article.

[lens/intent-preservation][lens/security] lib/topic_retriever.rb:15 — Remote-fetch validation compares only the hostname: non-HTTP schemes can pass, and resolved private/loopback addresses and redirect destinations are not checked, enabling protocol abuse, DNS rebinding, and redirect-based SSRF.
app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:10 — The change adds an independently scheduled RSS/Atom ingestion system, settings, and dependencies, materially expanding beyond embed URL handling and validation.
lib/tasks/disqus.thor:116 — The existing Disqus importer’s `--category` option and category assignment are removed, an unrelated breaking change.
db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3 — Adding `force: true` to the unrelated existing `top_topics` migration unnecessarily permits destructive table recreation.
app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:10 — Existing embeds are resolved before validating the submitted URL’s host, allowing an authorized referrer to request an already-imported URL from another host.
lib/topic_retriever.rb:15 — Host comparison is case-sensitive even though DNS hostnames are case-insensitive, rejecting otherwise valid URLs with different casing.

app/models/topic_embed.rb:15 — Raw URLs are used as embed identities without canonicalization, so fragment, hostname-case, and default-port variants can create duplicate topics and bypass per-URL throttling.
lib/topic_retriever.rb:27 — The throttle performs `SETNX` and `EXPIRE` separately; a crash between them leaves the URL permanently throttled.

lib/topic_retriever.rb:40 — Every cache miss polls and imports the entire feed; the unbounded loop at `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:31` causes O(feed-size) parsing and per-item database work for each requested URL.

app/models/topic_embed.rb:15 — Import uses check-then-insert without conflict handling; concurrent workers can both create posts, with one failing on the unique index and aborting the no-retry poll batch.
app/models/post.rb:133 — `raw_html` persists for the post’s lifetime, so later ordinary revisions continue bypassing the rendering pipeline even when the content is no longer a trusted import.
db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:4 — Required `topic_id` and `post_id` lack foreign keys or deletion semantics, permitting orphaned embeds and lookups referencing nonexistent topics.

app/models/topic_embed.rb:13 — Stored XSS: attacker-controlled URL and RSS content are stored with `skip_validations: true` and `cook_method: :raw_html`, returned unchanged by `Post#cook`, and rendered with `raw post.cooked`.

app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:15 — Unauthenticated requests enqueue jobs before worker-side validation or throttling; unlimited distinct URLs can flood Sidekiq and trigger outbound retrieval/topic creation.

app/assets/javascripts/embed.js:17 — `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin)` uses substring matching instead of exact origin equality, allowing a lookalike prefix origin to send resize messages and manipulate the embedding page’s layout.

goldens.comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Missing test changes or validation evidence for changed source files: `lib/post_creator.rb`, `lib/post_revisor.rb`, `lib/tasks/disqus.thor`, and `lib/topic_retriever.rb`.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims there are missing tests for lib/post_creator.rb, lib/post_revisor.rb, lib/tasks/disqus.thor, and lib/topic_retriever.rb. Looking at the diff: 1) lib/topic_retriever.rb has a corresponding test file spec/components/topic_retriever_spec.rb added. 2) The changes to lib/post_creator.rb and lib/post_revisor.rb are small additions (cook_method handling and skip_validations option) that are exercised through the TopicEmbed tests in spec/models/topic_embed_spec.rb which tests the import functionality that uses PostCreator with cook_method. 3) lib/tasks/disqus.thor is a Thor task file for manual imports, not typically requiring unit tests. The finding is overly broad - topic_retriever.rb does have tests, and the other changes are integration-tested through TopicEmbed specs. This is not a real defect but rather a style/coverage preference.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 — `import_remote` uses `open(url)` without requiring `open-uri` on the normal retrieval path, so HTTP URLs may be treated as local filenames.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in app/models/topic_embed.rb line 48, the `import_remote` method calls `open(url).read`. The `open-uri` gem is required in app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb (line 7: `require 'open-uri'`), but NOT in app/models/topic_embed.rb. The `import_remote` method can be called from multiple paths: 1) from `TopicRetriever#fetch_http` (lib/topic_retriever.rb line 52), and 2) from the disqus import task. When called via TopicRetriever, `open-uri` is not required beforehand. Without `open-uri`, `Kernel#open` with a URL string would try to open it as a local file path, which would fail or potentially be a security issue. This is a real bug - the `require 'open-uri'` should be in topic_embed.rb or at the top of the file that uses `open(url)`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [lens/completeness] spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:43 — The test expects synchronous `TopicRetriever.new(...).retrieve`, while the controller now enqueues `:retrieve_topic`; the test fails and does not validate the asynchronous handoff.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the test in spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb lines 41-47, it expects TopicRetriever.new to be called and then retrieve to be called on it. However, looking at the controller in app/controllers/embed_controller.rb lines 13-15, when topic_id is nil, it calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, user_id: current_user.try(:id), embed_url: embed_url)` - it enqueues a job rather than directly calling TopicRetriever. The test mocks TopicRetriever.expects(:new).returns(retriever) and retriever.expects(:retrieve), but the controller never directly instantiates TopicRetriever - it enqueues a job. The job (app/jobs/regular/retrieve_topic.rb) is what eventually calls TopicRetriever. So the test's expectations don't match the actual controller behavior - the test would fail because TopicRetriever.new is never called directly by the controller.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:11 — URL validation checks only an `http(s)://` prefix, so malformed values such as `http://[` pass and later raise instead of being rejected cleanly.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff in app/models/topic_embed.rb line 11, the import method has: `return unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//`. This regex only checks that the URL starts with 'http://' or 'https://', but doesn't validate the full URL structure. A malformed URL like 'http://[' would pass this check but could cause issues later when parsed by URI() in the absolutize_urls method (lines 52-53). The absolutize_urls method does `uri = URI(url)` which would raise URI::InvalidURIError for malformed URLs. However, looking at the code flow, import() is called and if the URL passes the regex check, it proceeds to create content and potentially call absolutize_urls. The finding is valid - the validation is insufficient and malformed URLs that pass the regex could cause exceptions later rather than being cleanly rejected upfront.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:64 — URL absolutization handles only root-relative paths; document-relative references such as `article/2`, `../images/x.png`, and `?page=2` resolve against Discourse instead of the source article.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the absolutize_urls method in app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 52-70, the code only handles URLs that start with '/': `if href.present? && href.start_with?('/')`. This means document-relative URLs like 'article/2', '../images/x.png', or '?page=2' would not be converted to absolute URLs. These relative URLs would remain as-is and would resolve against the Discourse domain instead of the original source article domain. This is a real correctness issue - when importing content from external sources, relative URLs that don't start with '/' will be broken.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [lens/intent-preservation][lens/security] lib/topic_retriever.rb:15 — Remote-fetch validation compares only the hostname: non-HTTP schemes can pass, and resolved private/loopback addresses and redirect destinations are not checked, enabling protocol abuse, DNS rebinding, and redirect-based SSRF.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, lib/topic_retriever.rb:15 shows `invalid_host?` method that only checks `SiteSetting.embeddable_host != URI(@embed_url).host`. This validation is indeed weak - it only compares hostnames and doesn't validate the scheme (allowing file://, gopher://, etc.), doesn't check for private/loopback IPs, and doesn't handle redirects. The `fetch_http` method at line 49 calls `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, @embed_url)` which in topic_embed.rb uses `open(url).read` (via ruby-readability). The `open-uri` library in Ruby can follow redirects and access various protocols. This is a real SSRF vulnerability - an attacker could potentially access internal services by: 1) Using non-HTTP schemes, 2) Using hostnames that resolve to internal IPs, 3) Exploiting redirects from the allowed host to internal resources. The finding correctly identifies a security issue in the URL validation logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:10 — The change adds an independently scheduled RSS/Atom ingestion system, settings, and dependencies, materially expanding beyond embed URL handling and validation.

adjudication.rationale: The finding describes the addition of a new RSS/Atom feed polling system as 'materially expanding beyond embed URL handling'. However, this is not a bug, security issue, or correctness problem - it's a description of new functionality being added. The code in poll_feed.rb is intentionally adding scheduled RSS feed polling as part of the embedding feature set. This is a feature addition, not a defect. The finding reads more like a scope observation than an actual problem with the code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/tasks/disqus.thor:116 — The existing Disqus importer’s `--category` option and category assignment are removed, an unrelated breaking change.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for lib/tasks/disqus.thor, the `--category` option is indeed removed from line 117 (method_option :category), and the category_id logic is removed from the import method (lines 144-147 in the original). The PostCreator call is replaced with TopicEmbed.import_remote which doesn't accept a category parameter. This is a breaking change for users who relied on the --category flag to import Disqus comments into a specific category. The finding correctly identifies that existing functionality is being removed without replacement.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3 — Adding `force: true` to the unrelated existing `top_topics` migration unnecessarily permits destructive table recreation.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb, the change is from `create_table :top_topics do |t|` to `create_table :top_topics, force: true do |t|`. The finding claims this is 'unnecessary' and 'permits destructive table recreation'. However, this is a migration file - migrations are typically run once and tracked. Adding `force: true` means if the table already exists, it will be dropped and recreated. This could be problematic in production if the migration is somehow re-run, but in normal Rails migration workflow, this wouldn't happen. The change appears intentional (perhaps to handle development scenarios where the table might exist). While `force: true` in migrations is generally not best practice for production safety, this is more of a style/best practice concern rather than a clear bug or defect. The migration would work correctly in normal usage.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:10 — Existing embeds are resolved before validating the submitted URL’s host, allowing an authorized referrer to request an already-imported URL from another host.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the embed_controller.rb code, the `ensure_embeddable` before_filter runs before the `best` action. This filter checks that `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` is set and that `request.referer` host matches `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The `best` action then calls `TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed(embed_url)` which simply looks up any existing embed by URL. The finding claims that an authorized referrer can request an already-imported URL from another host. However, looking at the import flow in `topic_embed.rb`, the `import` method only validates that the URL starts with `http://` or `https://` - it doesn't validate against `embeddable_host`. The `TopicRetriever` does validate the host in `invalid_host?` method. So if content was imported via RSS feed polling (which doesn't validate host), an embed from a different host could exist in the database. When a user with valid referer requests that embed_url, they would get the topic_id and see the content. This is a valid security concern - the embed lookup doesn't verify the embed_url belongs to the embeddable_host, only that the referer is from the embeddable_host.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:15 — Host comparison is case-sensitive even though DNS hostnames are case-insensitive, rejecting otherwise valid URLs with different casing.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb:15, the code is `SiteSetting.embeddable_host != URI(@embed_url).host`. The URI.host method in Ruby returns the host portion of a URL, and DNS hostnames are indeed case-insensitive per RFC standards. If a user configures embeddable_host as 'EvilTrout.com' but the embed URL contains 'eviltrout.com', or vice versa, the comparison would fail even though they refer to the same host. This is a real correctness bug - the comparison should use case-insensitive matching (e.g., using downcase on both sides). This could cause valid embed URLs to be rejected.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:15 — Raw URLs are used as embed identities without canonicalization, so fragment, hostname-case, and default-port variants can create duplicate topics and bypass per-URL throttling.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, TopicEmbed.import() uses the embed_url directly without any canonicalization. The URL is used as-is in TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url) queries and stored directly. This means 'http://example.com/page' vs 'http://example.com/page#section' vs 'http://EXAMPLE.com/page' vs 'http://example.com:80/page' would all be treated as different URLs, potentially creating duplicate topics for the same content. The topic_id_for_embed method also uses the raw embed_url for lookups. This is a real correctness issue - URL variants that point to the same content would bypass deduplication and could create multiple topics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:27 — The throttle performs `SETNX` and `EXPIRE` separately; a crash between them leaves the URL permanently throttled.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb lines 25-31, the code does `$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` followed by `$redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60)` as separate operations. If the process crashes between these two calls, the key will exist without an expiration, meaning that URL would be permanently throttled (the key would never expire). This is a real race condition/reliability bug. The proper fix would be to use `SET key value EX 60 NX` (a single atomic operation) or use `SETEX` with appropriate logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:40 — Every cache miss polls and imports the entire feed; the unbounded loop at `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:31` causes O(feed-size) parsing and per-item database work for each requested URL.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code flow: when `perform_retrieve` is called in topic_retriever.rb, it checks if feed_polling_enabled and then calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` at line 40-41. The PollFeed job's `poll_feed` method at lines 23-35 iterates through ALL items in the RSS feed with `rss.items.each` and calls `TopicEmbed.import` for each one. This means every time a user requests an embed URL that isn't cached, the entire RSS feed is parsed and potentially imported. However, the `TopicEmbed.import` method does check if an embed already exists (`embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first`) and only creates new topics for new URLs. So while there is repeated work (fetching and parsing the feed, checking each URL), it's not creating duplicate content. The finding is partially correct - there is inefficiency in re-polling the entire feed on cache misses, but the 'unbounded loop' concern is mitigated by the existing-embed check. The real issue is the repeated HTTP fetch and parse of the feed, not truly O(feed-size) database work since most items will already exist.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:15 — Import uses check-then-insert without conflict handling; concurrent workers can both create posts, with one failing on the unique index and aborting the no-retry poll batch.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb, the import method does check `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and then creates a new TopicEmbed if blank. This is indeed a check-then-insert pattern. However, examining the context: 1) The code is wrapped in `Topic.transaction`, 2) There's a unique index on embed_url (from the migration), 3) The TopicRetriever also has a check `return if TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: @embed_url).exists?` before calling import. While there is a theoretical race condition, the finding claims this would cause 'one failing on the unique index and aborting the no-retry poll batch'. Looking at poll_feed.rb, it iterates through RSS items and calls TopicEmbed.import for each. If one fails due to a unique constraint violation, it would raise an exception. The job has `sidekiq_options retry: false`, so it wouldn't retry. This is a real race condition that could cause data integrity issues or job failures in concurrent scenarios.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/post.rb:133 — `raw_html` persists for the post’s lifetime, so later ordinary revisions continue bypassing the rendering pipeline even when the content is no longer a trusted import.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, when a post is created via TopicEmbed.import(), it sets cook_method to Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]. This is stored in the database (see migration adding cook_method column). When PostRevisor.revise! is called for updates, it calls @post.save but does NOT reset cook_method. The finding claims that if someone later edits the post through normal means (not via import), the raw_html cook_method persists and bypasses the rendering pipeline. However, examining the code flow: PostRevisor doesn't change cook_method, so it stays as raw_html. But this is actually the intended behavior for imported content - it should remain raw HTML. The real question is whether a user could manually edit an imported post and have their potentially malicious content bypass sanitization. Looking at post.rb line 131-133, if cook_method is raw_html, it returns raw directly without cooking. This means any subsequent edits to that post would also bypass cooking/sanitization. This is a legitimate security concern - if a staff member or the post owner edits an imported post, their new content would be rendered as raw HTML without sanitization.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:4 — Required `topic_id` and `post_id` lack foreign keys or deletion semantics, permitting orphaned embeds and lookups referencing nonexistent topics.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points out that the migration creates topic_id and post_id columns without foreign key constraints. Looking at the migration in db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb, it creates columns with `null: false` but no foreign key constraints. However, this is a common Rails pattern - Rails applications typically handle referential integrity at the application level rather than database level. The TopicEmbed model has `belongs_to :topic` and `belongs_to :post` associations. While adding foreign keys would be better practice, the lack of database-level foreign keys is not a bug or defect - it's a design choice consistent with Rails conventions. The code will function correctly; orphaned records would only occur if topics/posts are deleted without cleaning up embeds, which is a separate concern. This is more of a best practice suggestion than a real defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:13 — Stored XSS: attacker-controlled URL and RSS content are stored with `skip_validations: true` and `cook_method: :raw_html`, returned unchanged by `Post#cook`, and rendered with `raw post.cooked`.
matched_golden_ids: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the XSS vulnerability related to attacker-controlled URL and content being stored and rendered unsafely, which matches part of the golden comment about 'XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML'. However, the candidate does not mention the NoMethodError issue when contents parameter is nil. The golden comment identifies TWO issues (NoMethodError AND XSS), while the candidate only identifies one (XSS). Since the candidate partially matches by identifying the XSS vulnerability, but misses the NoMethodError issue, this is a partial match. The question is whether identifying the same underlying issue means both issues or just one. Since the golden comment treats these as a combined issue description, and the candidate only catches half of it, I'll consider this a partial match with moderate confidence.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:15 — Unauthenticated requests enqueue jobs before worker-side validation or throttling; unlimited distinct URLs can flood Sidekiq and trigger outbound retrieval/topic creation.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the embed_controller.rb, the `best` action at line 15 calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` when no existing topic_id is found. The `ensure_embeddable` before_filter does validate that the referer host matches `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`, which provides some protection. However, the TopicRetriever class does implement throttling via Redis (`retrieved_recently?` method) that limits retrieval to once per 60 seconds per URL. Additionally, staff users bypass this throttle (`no_throttle: user.try(:staff?)`). For unauthenticated users (current_user is nil), the throttle applies. The finding claims 'unlimited distinct URLs can flood Sidekiq' - while jobs are enqueued, the actual retrieval is throttled per-URL. However, the job enqueueing itself is not throttled, so an attacker could enqueue many jobs for different URLs. The worker-side throttling in TopicRetriever would prevent actual HTTP fetches for recently-retrieved URLs, but new unique URLs would still trigger outbound requests. This is a legitimate concern - the rate limiting happens at the worker level, not at the controller level, allowing job queue flooding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/embed.js:17 — `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin)` uses substring matching instead of exact origin equality, allowing a lookalike prefix origin to send resize messages and manipulate the embedding page’s layout.

Both point out that using indexOf for origin validation is insufficient because it uses substring matching instead of exact equality, which allows malicious domains to bypass the check. The golden comment gives the example of 'evil-discourseUrl.com' while the candidate describes it as 'lookalike prefix origin' - both are describing the same bypass technique where a malicious domain containing the legitimate domain as a substring could pass the validation.
